summary: This document specifies how to encapsulate ATM cells in a pseudowire carried over an MPLS network, along with the procedures for using such a pseudowire to provide an ATM service. This lets service providers offer emulated ATM services over existing MPLS networks.

plainLanguage.summary: ATM networks carry fixed 53-byte cells, while MPLS carries variable-length packets. This RFC defines how to carry an ATM service across an MPLS packet network: the ATM cells are placed in packets with a small header, and the two provider edge routers take over the switching that the ATM network would have done. It defines four ways to package the cells, and the rules for each.

questions: how does atm over mpls work
what is the pseudowire control word
subtitle: How ATM cells are carried across an MPLS packet network in a pseudowire.

tldr.problem: ATM networks carry fixed 53-byte cells while MPLS carries variable-length packets, so an ATM service cannot simply be run across an MPLS core without rules for packaging the cells and telling the two ends what they are carrying.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the general encapsulation format, a transport header, a pseudowire header, a control word and the ATM payload, plus four packaging modes: N-to-one cell mode, one-to-one cell mode, AAL5 SDU frame mode and AAL5 PDU frame mode.
tldr.outcome: A service provider can offer emulated ATM over an existing MPLS network, with the customer equipment unaware that the service is emulated. The RFC is explicit that this is not a perfect reproduction of native ATM: cell ordering is optional, ATM flow control cannot see the state of the packet network, and the security of the service is only as good as the security of the packet network.

facts.label: Control word size
facts.value: 4 bytes, for both the generic and the preferred control word

facts.label: Sequence number
facts.value: 16 bits, with the value 0 meaning the check is not used

facts.label: Length field
facts.value: 6 bits in the preferred control word, set to the packet length when it is under 64 bytes

facts.label: MTU headroom with MPLS
facts.value: 12 or more bytes above the largest frame size

facts.label: Concatenated cells limit
facts.value: Set by the 0x02 interface parameter sub-TLV, a 2-octet value

today: RFC 4717 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification for carrying ATM services over MPLS pseudowires, and its encapsulations are identical to those in the ITU-T Y.1411 and Y.1412 recommendations.

sections.title: What the Specification Covers
sections.content:
Packet-switched networks have the potential to reduce the complexity of a service provider's infrastructure by allowing virtually any existing digital service to be supported over a single networking infrastructure. The benefit is threefold: leveraging existing systems and services to provide increased capacity from a packet-switched core; preserving existing network operational processes used to maintain the legacy services; and using the common packet-switched network infrastructure to support both the capacity requirements of existing services and the requirements of new services supported natively over the packet network.

This document describes a method to carry ATM services over MPLS. It lists ATM-specific requirements and provides encapsulation formats and semantics for connecting ATM edge networks through a packet-switched network using MPLS. In the reference model, a customer edge device is where one end of a service originates or terminates, and it is not aware that it is using an emulated service rather than a native one. A provider edge device provides the emulation to the customer edge. A pseudowire is the connection between two provider edge routers carried over the packet-switched network, and a pseudowire PDU is the packet sent on it containing all the data and control information needed to provide the service.

The ATM over pseudowire service is not intended to perfectly emulate a traditional ATM service, but it can be used for applications that need an ATM transport service. The notable differences are these. ATM cell ordering can be preserved using the optional sequence field in the control word, but implementations are not required to support it, and its use may impact other ATM quality of service commitments. The quality of service model for traditional ATM can be emulated, but the detailed specification of that emulation is outside the scope of the document. The ATM flow control mechanisms are transparent to the MPLS network and cannot reflect the status of the MPLS network. Control plane support for ATM switched virtual circuits, switched virtual paths, soft-signalled PVCs and soft-signalled PVPs is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Packet-switched networks let a provider run several kinds of service over one network. This document describes how to carry ATM services over MPLS. The customer's devices talk to provider edge routers as before, and those routers pass the service over a pseudowire inside a tunnel, so the customer does not know the service is emulated. The RFC is clear that this is not a perfect copy of native ATM: cell ordering is optional, ATM flow control cannot see the state of the packet network, and signalling support is out of scope.

sections.title: The General Encapsulation Format
sections.content:
Each packet sent on a pseudowire has a PSN Transport Header, a Pseudowire Header, an ATM Control Word and an ATM Service Payload.

The PSN Transport Header depends on the particular tunnelling technology in use, and it is used to transport the encapsulated ATM information through the packet-switched core. The Pseudowire Header identifies a particular ATM service on a tunnel; in the case of MPLS, the pseudowire header is one or more MPLS labels at the bottom of the MPLS label stack. The ATM Control Word is inserted before the ATM service payload, and it may contain a length and sequence number in addition to the control bits needed to carry the service.

Two kinds of traffic direction are used throughout the document. The PSN Bound direction is where information from a customer edge is adapted to a pseudowire and pseudowire PDUs are sent into the packet-switched network. The CE Bound direction is where pseudowire PDUs are received from the network, re-converted back into the emulated service and sent out to a customer edge. Ingress is the point where the ATM service is encapsulated into a pseudowire PDU, and egress is the point where it is decapsulated from one.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has three parts on top of the tunnel header. The pseudowire header identifies which ATM service the packet belongs to; in MPLS that is one or more labels at the bottom of the label stack. The control word comes next, a fixed header that can carry a length, a sequence number and some control bits. The ATM payload follows, holding the cells.

sections.title: The Control Word
sections.content:
The control words in this document are based on the Generic PW MPLS Control Word. They provide the ability to sequence individual frames on the pseudowire, avoidance of equal-cost multiple-path load-balancing, and operations mechanisms including VCCV.

The reason for the control word is specific. If a pseudowire is sensitive to packet misordering and is carried over an MPLS network that uses the contents of the MPLS payload to select the equal-cost path, it must employ a mechanism that prevents packet misordering, because equal-cost implementations may examine the first nibble after the MPLS label stack to determine whether the labelled packet is IP. If the VPI of an ATM connection carried in N-to-one cell mode without a control word begins with 0x4 or 0x6, it could be mistaken for an IPv4 or IPv6 packet, which could lead to all the packets for a given pseudowire not following the same path, increasing out-of-order frames or sending operations packets down a different path than the real traffic.

Two control words are defined. The generic control word is used in ATM One-to-one Cell Mode and AAL5 PDU Frame Mode. Its first 4 bits MUST be set to 0 to indicate pseudowire data and MUST be ignored on receipt. The next 4 bits are reserved and MUST be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on reception. The next 16 bits are a sequence number that can be used to guarantee ordered packet delivery, and the processing of the sequence number field is OPTIONAL. The sequence number space is a 16-bit unsigned circular space, and the value 0 is used to indicate that the sequence number check algorithm is not used. The last 8 bits provide space for ATM-specific flags.

The preferred control word is used in ATM N-to-one Cell Mode and AAL5 SDU Frame Mode. It has the same four leading zero bits, then 4 bits of protocol-specific flags, then 2 reserved bits, then a 6-bit length field, then the 16-bit sequence number. The length field is used as follows: if the packet's length, defined as the length of the layer 2 payload plus the length of the control word, is less than 64 bytes, the length field MUST be set to the packet's length; otherwise it MUST be set to zero. A non-zero value can be used to remove any padding added by a link with a minimum frame size. The length field is not used in N-to-one mode and MUST be set to 0 there.

The control word provides little value when the features it offers are not needed, so it is OPTIONAL in general, but future implementations MUST be able to send and receive frames without a control word present, for backwards compatibility with early deployments. In all cases the egress router must know whether the ingress router will send a control word on a specific pseudowire, which may be achieved by configuration or by signalling.
sections.plainLanguage: The control word stops an ATM cell from being mistaken for an IP packet. MPLS networks that spread traffic over equal-cost paths look at the first nibble after the label stack, so a cell whose VPI starts with 4 or 6 could be sent down a different path. The control word also lets the receiver order frames and remove padding. Two versions exist, both four bytes: the generic one, with a 16-bit sequence number and eight ATM-specific bits, and the preferred one, which adds four flag bits and a six-bit length field. A sequence number of zero means the ordering check is off. The control word is optional, but implementations must cope with frames that have none.

sections.title: MTU, the Label Stack and TTL
sections.content:
The network MUST be configured with an MTU that is sufficient to transport the largest encapsulation frames. If MPLS is used as the tunnelling protocol, this is likely to be 12 or more bytes greater than the largest frame size, and other tunnelling protocols may have longer headers and require larger MTUs. If the ingress router determines that an encapsulated layer 2 PDU exceeds the MTU of the tunnel through which it must be sent, the PDU MUST be dropped. If an egress router receives an encapsulated layer 2 PDU whose payload length, the length of the PDU itself without any of the encapsulation headers, exceeds the MTU of the destination layer 2 interface, the PDU MUST be dropped.

The ingress label switching router MUST set the S bit of the pseudowire label to a value of 1, to denote that the VC label is at the bottom of the stack. The setting of the TTL value in the pseudowire label is application dependent, but the MPLS TTL processing procedure, including handling of expired TTLs, MUST be followed.
sections.plainLanguage: The network has to be configured with an MTU big enough for the largest encapsulated frame. With MPLS tunnelling that is likely 12 or more bytes more than the largest frame, and other tunnelling protocols need more. If the ingress router finds the packet too big for the tunnel it must drop it, and the egress router must drop a packet whose payload is too big for the destination interface. The ingress router sets the bottom-of-stack bit in the pseudowire label to 1, and the usual MPLS TTL rules apply.

sections.title: The Four Packaging Modes
sections.content:
Two methods are defined for the encapsulation of ATM cells. The N-to-one mode, where N is at least 1, maps one or more ATM virtual channel connections, or one or more virtual path connections, to one pseudowire. It is the only REQUIRED mode. One format is used for both the VCC or VPC mapping to the tunnel, the 4-octet ATM header is unaltered in the encapsulation so the VPI and VCI are always present, and cells from one or more VCCs or VPCs may be concatenated. The encapsulation supports all ATM Adaptation Layer types, and non-terminating OAM and admin cells are transported among the user cells in the same order as they are received, which enables performance management and security applications.

The One-to-one mode maps one ATM VCC, or one ATM VPC, to one pseudowire. For VCCs the VPI and VCI are not included and for VPCs the VPI is not included, because only one connection is carried on the pseudowire and those fields can be derived from the context of the pseudowire label. The mode uses less bandwidth than N-to-one for a given number of concatenated cells. It is OPTIONAL.

Two further OPTIONAL encapsulations carry ATM AAL5 transport. The AAL5 SDU frame encapsulation allows the transport of AAL5 service data units travelling on a particular ATM PVC across the network to another ATM PVC, and is used by a pseudowire of type 0x0002, ATM AAL5 SDU VCC transport. It is more efficient for small AAL5 SDUs than the cell encapsulations, and it requires segmentation and reassembly on the PE to CE ATM interface. Its limitations are that an OAM cell received at the ingress router is sent before the cells of the surrounding AAL5 frame, so OAM cell reordering may occur; a scrambled AAL5 PDU cannot be read by the router and the whole PDU will be dropped; the AAL5 PDU CRC is not transported across the packet network and must be regenerated at the egress router; the length of an AAL5 frame may exceed the MTU of the network and require fragmentation; and the mode does not preserve the CLP bit or the EFCI state for every cell within an AAL5 PDU.

The AAL5 PDU frame encapsulation is used for the transparent carriage of ATM layer services that use AAL5 to carry higher-layer frames, and its main advantage is that it is transparent to ATM OAM and ATM security applications. The whole AAL5 PDU is encapsulated, so all necessary parameters, CPCS-UU, CPI, Length and CRC, are transported as part of the payload. Because the whole PDU is carried, fragmentation is performed at cell boundaries and the CRC in the trailer can be used to check the integrity of the PDU, and reassembly is not required at the egress router for the packet to ATM direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Four packaging modes are defined. N-to-one cell mode is the only required one: it carries several virtual channel or virtual path connections over one pseudowire and leaves the 4-byte ATM header in place. One-to-one cell mode is optional and carries a single connection, taking the VCI and VPI from the label instead, so it uses less bandwidth. Two optional modes carry AAL5 traffic: the SDU mode sends the reassembled frame, which is efficient for small frames but loses OAM cell order and regenerates the CRC at the far end; the PDU mode sends the whole AAL5 PDU, which keeps OAM and security applications transparent.

sections.title: Operations Cells and the ATM Management Interface
sections.content:
When configured for ATM VCC service, both provider edge routers SHOULD act as a VC switch in accordance with the OAM procedures defined in ITU-T I.610. The routers SHOULD be able to pass the F5 Alarm Indication Signal, segment and end to end, the F5 Remote Defect Indicator, segment and end to end, and F5 loopback transparently. Separate procedures apply in the VPC case, and there is a separate emulation mode for SDU and PDU OAM cells.

An MPLS edge router MAY provide an ATM Integrated Local Management Interface to the ATM edge switch. If an ingress router receives an ILMI message indicating that the ATM edge switch has deleted a VC, or if the physical interface goes down, it MUST send a pseudowire status notification message for all the pseudowires associated with the failure. When a pseudowire label mapping is withdrawn, or a status notification message is received, the egress router MUST notify its client of the failure by deleting the VC using ILMI.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider edge routers should act as a virtual channel switch for the operations cells of the emulated service, and pass the alarm indication, remote defect indicator and loopback cells transparently. The provider edge router may also offer an ATM management interface to the customer's ATM switch; if that interface reports a deleted connection, or the physical link goes down, the ingress router must send a status message for every pseudowire affected, and the egress router must then delete the connection on the customer side.

sections.title: Class of Service and Congestion
sections.content:
The ATM service category of a connection SHOULD be mapped to a compatible class of service in the packet-switched network, and a compatible class of service maintains the integrity of the service end to end. For example, the CBR service category SHOULD be mapped to a class of service with stringent loss and delay objectives, and if the network implements the IP Diffserv framework a class of service based on the EF PHB is a good candidate. Some ATM service categories are CLP blind, such as CBR, meaning that the quality objectives apply to the aggregate cell flow, and some are CLP significant, such as VBR.3. When the packet network is MPLS based, a mapping between the CLP bit and the EXP field can be performed to provide visibility of the cell loss priority in the MPLS network. This section is provided for informational purposes and guidance only.

The packet-switched network carrying the pseudowire may be subject to congestion, and during congestion it may exhibit packet loss that impacts the ATM service. Because ATM pseudowires carry a variety of services across the network, including but not restricted to TCP/IP, they may or may not behave in a TCP-friendly manner, and in the presence of services that reduce their transmission rate they may consume more than their fair share, in which case they SHOULD be halted. Whenever possible, ATM pseudowires should be run over traffic-engineered packet networks providing bandwidth allocation and admission control, such as domains offering Guaranteed Service or domains using expedited forwarding. The routers SHOULD monitor for congestion, using explicit congestion notification or by measuring packet loss, so that the service may be maintained.
sections.plainLanguage: The ATM service category of a connection should be mapped to a compatible class of service in the packet network, for example a constant bit rate connection to a class with tight loss and delay objectives. When the packet network uses Diffserv, an expedited forwarding class is a good candidate, and when the network is MPLS based the cell loss priority bit can be mapped to the MPLS EXP field. The packet network may also be congested, and the RFC suggests running ATM pseudowires over traffic-engineered networks with bandwidth allocation and admission control, and having the routers monitor for congestion.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document specifies only encapsulations, not the protocols used to carry the encapsulated packets across the packet-switched network. Each such protocol may have its own set of security issues, but those issues are not affected by the encapsulations specified here. The security of the transported ATM service will only be as good as the security of the packet-switched network, and this level of security might be less rigorous than that of a native ATM service.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC specifies only the encapsulations, not the protocol that carries them across the packet network. The security of the emulated ATM service is only as good as the security of the packet network, which may be less rigorous than that of a native ATM service.

fields.desc: Must be 0 to indicate pseudowire data, and must be ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: The packet length if it is under 64 bytes, otherwise zero. A non-zero value lets the receiver strip padding.

fields.desc: A 16-bit circular number used to guarantee ordered delivery. The value 0 means the check is not used.

items.title: Cell ordering
items.text: Can be preserved with the optional sequence field, but implementations are not required to support it.

items.title: Quality of service
items.text: The ATM model can be emulated, but the detailed emulation is outside the scope of the document.

items.title: Flow control
items.text: ATM flow control is transparent to the MPLS network and cannot reflect the state of that network.

items.title: Signalling
items.text: Control plane support for ATM switched and soft-signalled connections is out of scope.
